sources.title: Amrita Sher-Gil (Q150312) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-24): English label 'Amrita Sher-Gil', description 'Hungarian-Indian painter (1913-1941)', Korean label '암리타 셰르길', born 30 January 1913, died 5 December 1941, citizenship British Raj. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi, virtual tour 'An Unfinished Journey | Amrita Sher-Gil' (ngmaindia.gov.in), read in full including the dated chronology and the curatorial essay: training in Paris from 1929 (Grande Chaumiere under Pierre Vaillant, then Lucien Simon at the Ecole Nationale des Beaux-Arts); Young Girls (1932) wins a gold medal at the Grand Salon and an associate membership; her return to India in December 1934; in September 1935 she rejects an award of the Simla Fine Art Society; exhibitions at the Taj Mahal Hotel in Bombay (1936), Hyderabad, Allahabad University, the Imperial Hotel in New Delhi and in Lahore (1937); a gold medal at the Bombay Art Society in January 1937; travels to Ajanta, Ellora and the Mattancheri frescoes in Cochin, and introduction to Pahari, Basholi, Rajput and Mughal miniatures through Karl Khandalavala; the South Indian paintings of 1937 (Brahmacharis, Bride's Toilet, South Indian Villagers Going to Market); an unfinished last painting in Lahore in 1941; the curatorial text calls her place in the trajectory of Indian modern art 'unquestionably pre eminent', her aesthetic a blend of European and Indian elements, and quotes her essay 'Evolution of My Art' (self). The gallery holds 103 of her works. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Institutional, admiring, built partly on her own letters and writings; the entries on her marriage, relatives and death were not used.

'Biography', Global Modern Women Artists: Amrita Sher-Gil (Smith College, sites.smith.edu), read in full: an academic summary citing Yashodhara Dalmia's biography and other scholars: Paris training at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and exposure to Van Gogh, Cezanne and Modigliani; return to India in 1934 with the stated view that an Ajanta fresco or a piece of sculpture in the Musee Guimet is worth more than the whole Renaissance; her stated aim to be an interpreter of the life of the poor through line, colour and design; from 1934 a blending of Eastern and Western styles with simplified form and colour; she was criticised for Western influence and her departure from the Bengal School, and her paintings did not sell as well as she wanted; later use of Mughal miniature elements and experiments with three-dimensional forms and animal subjects. Student-built academic site, secondary and partly relying on one biography; its passages on love affairs, marriage, health and death were not used.

Salman Rushdie, review/introduction to 'Amrita Sher-Gil: A Self-Portrait in Letters and Writings' (ed. Vivan Sundaram, Tulika Books, 2010), first published in The Guardian in 2007 and reprinted by SikhNet on 1 October 2010, read in full: an outside writer's reading of her letters, with quotations of her outspoken views (praise of Tagore with a barb, dismissal of the Bengal school as having 'only a shell', admiration for the Ajanta frescoes and the Cochin frescoes she copied, Breughel and Renoir as influences); an anecdote in her words that the Nizam of Hyderabad declined to buy two of her 'cubist' pictures after she questioned his taste; her argument to her father that Europe had led her to appreciate Indian art; Rushdie's judgement that her art moves toward melancholy and was often misunderstood. Admiring outside review built on her own letters (self material), a reprint rather than the original page; the family, love-life and death passages were not used.

'10 Indian Modernist Artists from the 20th Century You Should Know', Artsy editorial (artsy.net), the Amrita Sher-Gil entry read: best known for vivid and sympathetic portrayals of Indian rural life; formal education at the Ecole Nationale Superieure des Beaux-Arts from age 16; Indian miniature and cave-painting traditions meet the approaches of Cezanne, Gauguin and Modigliani; on returning in the mid-1930s she saw her creativity tied to India; paintings foreground women, such as Group of Three Girls (1935); 'one of India's most innovative and in demand modern artists'. Short market-oriented art-site editorial; used for the significance statement only.

Wikimedia Commons file pages for Amrita Sher-Gil images -- checked for the portrait: 'Amrita Sher-Gil 2.jpg' (the Wikidata image: 1936, author unknown, 'probably Umrao Singh Sher-Gil', source a Hungarian gallery website) and the self-portrait files 'Amrita Sher-Gil - Self-Portrait 1927.jpg' (pencil, 1927-10-04, source the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art site) and 'Self-portrait October 1937.jpg' (source: scan from Vivan Sundaram's 2010 book). Not used as support for any trait row.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_as_ngma, src_as_smith, src_as_artsy, src_as_rushdie | 1934-1941 | national-gallery chronology and essay + academic summary + art-site editorial + outside review] The National Gallery of Modern Art credits her with a mix of Western and Eastern traditions and describes her South Indian paintings of 1937 as a watershed; the Smith College summary says her work from 1934 began to blend Eastern and Western styles with simplified form and colour and that she was criticised for departing from the Bengal School; Artsy says Indian miniature and cave-painting traditions meet the approaches of Cezanne, Gauguin and Modigliani in her work; Rushdie reads her palette and melancholy as her own. Four independent but largely admiring sources describe a recognisably individual synthesis, with the critical reaction of the time recorded by one, so documented at a moderate confidence.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_as_ngma, src_as_smith, src_as_rushdie | 1929-1937 | national-gallery chronology + academic summary + outside review] The chronology records formal training from 1929 at the Grande Chaumiere and then in Lucien Simon's studio at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, prizes in Paris (a gold medal for Young Girls in 1932), later study of Ajanta, Ellora, the Cochin frescoes and Pahari, Basholi, Rajput and Mughal miniatures; the Smith summary adds exposure to Van Gogh, Cezanne and Modigliani; Rushdie quotes her letters on copying the Cochin frescoes to learn their technique (self). Sustained study of both European and Indian traditions is documented across sources; day-to-day working method is not described, so a moderate confidence.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_as_ngma, src_as_smith, src_as_rushdie | 1935-1937 | national-gallery chronology + academic summary + outside review] The chronology records that in September 1935 she rejected an award of the Simla Fine Art Society, and quotes her 1936 essay saying she resents 'outside interference' in her painting (self); the Smith summary says she was criticised for departing from the Bengal School and her paintings did not sell as well as she wanted; Rushdie reports her outspoken letters, including the anecdote of the Nizam of Hyderabad declining her pictures after she criticised his taste (her own account). Declining a local award and keeping to her own direction despite criticism is consistent with a strong need for independence, but the strongest statements are her own, so strong inference at a modest confidence, dual-edged because the stance cost her patrons. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 66 / 0.52 lowered to 62 / 0.46 because the main statements are her own words and the one outside behavioural fact is a single chronology entry.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_as_ngma, src_as_smith | 1934-1937 | national-gallery chronology + academic summary] The chronology records that she returned to India in December 1934 for her artistic development, travelled to Ajanta, Ellora, Cochin and Kerala, arranged exhibitions in hotels and halls in Bombay (1936), Hyderabad, Allahabad, New Delhi and Lahore (1937), and met the collector-critic Karl Khandalavala who introduced her to Indian miniatures; the Smith summary says she set out to be an interpreter of the life of the poor. Self-directed travel and a chain of exhibitions she organised are documented by two sources; how much she arranged herself rather than through family or friends is not stated, so a moderate score.

experimentation.rationale: [src_as_ngma, src_as_smith, src_as_rushdie | 1934-1940 | national-gallery chronology + academic summary + outside review] The Smith summary says she turned to Mughal miniature elements in her last years and began to experiment with three-dimensional forms and animal subjects; the chronology lists her moves from Parisian academic nudes and portraits to the South Indian group of 1937 and to the Saraya paintings of 1938-40; Rushdie quotes her letters on trying Indian frescoes as models. A shift of idiom after each new encounter is documented, but the sources give little on technical trial itself, so a modest score.

portrait.reason: No concretely rights-clear portrait was found. (1) The Wikidata image 'Amrita Sher-Gil 2.jpg' (a 1936 photograph, 1692 x 1788) is rejected: its Commons page gives the author only as 'unknown, probably Umrao Singh Sher-Gil' (a speculative attribution), the source is a Hungarian gallery website, and the public-domain tags rest on India's anonymous-photograph rule and the 1996 United States restoration date without any documented first publication, so the rights basis is a theory rather than a record. (2) Her own self-portraits (for example 'Self-Portrait 1927', pencil, source the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art website, and 'Self-portrait October 1937', scanned from Vivan Sundaram's 2010 book) are by an author who died in 1941, so they are public domain by term in the EU (life plus 70) and in India (life plus 60); the remaining doubt is the United States, where the Commons tags assert 'unpublished' status that is not documented, and the museum's own page for the 1927 drawing gave no reproduction terms when opened (the page showed no image or notice). Next step: a rights check of one self-portrait (for example the 1937 painting) through the National Gallery of Modern Art or the Sundaram book's publisher, or a dated first-publication record, then add the file as a likeness (a self-portrait by the sitter); alternatively a photograph with a named photographer who died before 1955 and a documented publication date.

SLUG/QID CHECK: no production or candidate file for slug amrita-sher-gil or QID Q150312 in the roster56 worktree. REGION: south_asia. She was born in Budapest to an Indian Sikh father and a Hungarian mother, but grew up in Shimla from 1921, her mature work (1934-41) and national significance are Indian (the National Gallery of Modern Art is her main collection), and repo precedents for Europe-/US-linked South Asians born in India (Khorana, Chandrasekhar) use south_asia; nationalityCodes IN only because Hungarian citizenship was not verified. VOCABULARY: occupations painter and artist, field art, tags innovator and nonconformist, archetypes creative_creator and independent_creator all have EN+KO labels. ZERO POLITICS: nothing political scored; the chronology's meetings with political figures and nationalist context were not used. DECEASED SUBJECT: no inference from her early death, its unclear cause, illness, relationships, marriage, family conflicts or mental state; those passages in the Smith, NGMA and Rushdie texts were excluded. PORTRAIT PREFLIGHT: result negative; see portrait.reason (held, no file saved). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: National Gallery of Modern Art virtual tour (https://ngmaindia.gov.in/virtual-tour-of-amrita-sher-gil.asp), read in full, with the Artsy editorial. READ (5 cited non-Wikidata sources): NGMA, Smith College biography, Rushdie review reprint, Artsy entry, plus Commons file pages. Also opened but not cited: Wander Women Project (popular summary), AstaGuru blog (auction house), Scroll article on her sculpture (gallery-supplied, with a date discrepancy), Sotheby's lot essay (promotional; its Sher-Gil quotations came from Dalmia's reader), Deccan Herald and Vadehra pages (no substantive text). Blocked: Britannica and the New York Times not attempted; Tate and Google Arts and Culture pages are script-rendered and returned no text. Not opened: Yashodhara Dalmia's biography, Vivan Sundaram's two-volume letters (reached only through the Rushdie review and NGMA), Goodreads reader reviews. PERSPECTIVES: the national gallery (institution), a college's academic summary of Dalmia, an outside novelist-reviewer (Rushdie) reading her letters, and an art-site editorial; COUNTER-VOICE: the critical reaction to her Western influence and Bengal School departure (Smith) and the Nizam's refusal (Rushdie, her own account); no hostile critic was read. LIMITATIONS: much of the behavioural detail comes from her own letters and essay via secondary writers, thin independent behavioural sources (only the NGMA chronology and Smith summary), so no row exceeds 72 or 0.60 and there are only five rows. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): rows reviewed were autonomy_need (her own words dominate; lowered 66/0.52 to 62/0.46), creative_originality (highest score; left unchanged because four sources agree and the criticism of the time is recorded) and proactive_agency (relies on a chronology; left unchanged at 62/0.50). No broad scoring problem flagged beyond the thin evidence base.
